Abstract

Background and Aims

While endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) is recommended in adult patients with fulminant myocarditis, the clinical impact of its timing is still unclear.

Methods Data were collected from 419 adult patients with clinically suspected fulminant myocarditis admitted to intensive care units across 36 tertiary centres in 15 countries worldwide. The diagnosis of myocarditis was histologically proven in 210 (50%) patients, either by EMB (n = 183, 44%) or by autopsy/explanted heart examination (n = 27, 6%), and clinically suspected cardiac magnetic reson­ ance imaging confirmed in 96 (23%) patients. The primary outcome of survival free of heart transplantation (HTx) or left ventricu­ lar assist device (LVAD) at 1 year was specifically compared between patients with early EMB (within 2 days after intensive care unit admission, n = 103) and delayed EMB (n = 80). A propensity score-weighted analysis was done to control for confounders.

Results Median age on admission was 40 (29–52) years, and 322 (77%) patients received temporary mechanical circulatory support. A total of 273 (65%) patients survived without HTx/LVAD. The primary outcome was significantly different between pa­ tients with early and delayed EMB (70% vs. 49%, P = .004). After propensity score weighting, the early EMB group still sig­ nificantly differed from the delayed EMB group in terms of survival free of HTx/LVAD (63% vs. 40%, P = .021). Moreover, early EMB was independently associated with a lower rate of death or HTx/LVAD at 1 year (odds ratio of 0.44; 95% con­ fidence interval: 0.22–0.86; P = .016).

Conclusions Endomyocardial biopsy should be broadly and promptly used in patients admitted to the intensive care unit for clinically suspected fulminant myocarditis.

## Introduction

Myocarditis is an inflammatory disease of the myocardium caused by a broad range of aetiologies, among which viral infection is thought to be the most frequent one.1–5 Fulminant myocarditis (FM) is defined as clinically suspected acute myocarditis requiring pharmacologic ther­ apy and/or temporary mechanical circulatory support (t-MCS).6,7

Clinical presentations can range from low cardiac output syndrome to refractory cardiogenic shock.6 The use of t-MCS such as venoar­ terial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) or Impella® is the current cornerstone of treatment.5,8–10 Expert con­ sensus and scientific statements recommend that an endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) should be performed as soon as possible in patients with clinically suspected FM5–7,11,12 because histology can affect the outcome, with giant cell myocarditis (GCM) portending the worst prognosis.10 In addition, a recent registry showed that patients with clinically suspected FM without EMB had a worse prognosis com­ pared with patients with EMB.13 Consequently, early EMB (within 2 days of admission) may be fundamental in rapidly identifying the cause of disease and guiding therapy. However, in real-world practice, EMB is performed in a limited number of cases due to the perceived risks of the procedure, physician inexperience, or spontaneous recovery be­ fore EMB.14 Contemporary data in patients with FM are therefore needed to better define outcomes and assess if early EMB is associated with more favourable outcomes.9,14–17 FULLMOON (Fulminant Myocarditis: Outcomes and long-term prognosis) is a retrospective international registry that was established to assess care bundles and myocarditis-related events and factors associated with outcomes in the current era of t-MCS. We aim to report survival free of heart transplantation (HTx) or long-term left ventricular assist device (LVAD) within 1 year after intensive care unit (ICU) admission and to specifically compare outcomes between patients who had early EMB and delayed EMB.

## Methods

Study design: patients The FULLMOON study is an international, multi-centre, retrospective co­ hort study conducted in 36 tertiary hospitals with prompt access to VA-ECMO across 15 countries. Centres were invited to participate if they average at least 20 VA-ECMO runs per year (see Supplementary data online, Table S1 for details on hospital characteristics). All participating centres obtained Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval in accordance with their local regulations and adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki. In France, which was the coordinating country, IRB approval was obtained by Hospital Foch (IRB-00012437 number 21-08-05).

Cases of clinically suspected FM were retrospectively identified from January 2008 to January 2020. Myocarditis was biopsy proven in 183 (44%) patients who represent the present study cohort. The diagnosis was based on the Dallas criteria (including both active myocarditis, in­ flammatory infiltrate plus cardiomyocyte necrosis, and borderline myo­ carditis and inflammatory infiltrate without necrosis).18 Of 236 patients without EMB-fulfilled ESC 2013 criteria for clinically suspected myocar­ ditis,5 96 had cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) findings in keeping with myocarditis according to the 2018 modified Lake Louise cri­ teria.19 Other differential diagnoses, including coronary artery disease through coronary angiography or computed tomography angiography, were excluded in these 236 patients. All cases were reviewed by three investigators (F.H., V.R., and M.S.). Clinically suspected FM was defined as (i) recent onset (≤30 days before admission) of signs and symptoms

of acute heart failure with evidence of new-onset left ventricular systolic dysfunction, (ii) haemodynamic instability requiring inotropes or vaso­ pressors, and/or t-MCS [VA-ECMO, Impella®, intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP), or combined t-MCS] within 7 days following ICU admis­ sion. Exclusion criteria included previously known cardiac disease, Takotsubo syndrome, sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy, peripartum car­ diomyopathy, HTx, and age < 16 years. The flow chart reporting the se­ lection of cases is reported in Figure 1.

Data collection Baseline data were collected from ICU admission and included age, sex, his­ tory of myocarditis or autoimmune disease, type and timing of onset of ini­ tial symptoms, electrocardiogram (ECG) description, sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) score,20 simplified acute physiology score (SAPS II),21 survival after VA-ECMO (SAVE) score,22 left ventricular ejec­ tion fraction (LVEF) on echocardiogram, and laboratory tests. Troponin va­ lues were expressed as the multiple of the upper reference limit (URL) for each laboratory.

We collected major myocarditis-related events such as cardiac arrest, ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias, high-grade atrioventricu­ lar conduction abnormalities, need for t-MCS, mechanical ventilation (MV), and renal replacement therapy (RRT). Complications included intracranial haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke, limb ischaemia, and tamponade. Tamponade was considered as related to EMB when it occurred within 48 h after the procedure. Additionally, any immuno­ modulatory therapy (IMT) received in the ICU was reported. Immunomodulatory therapy received within 48 h after ICU admission was defined as ‘early IMT’.

We collected patients’ vital status during ICU stay, at hospital discharge, 1-year post-ICU admission, and last available follow-up. The causes of death, dates of HTx or LVAD implantation, recurrence of myocarditis, and LVEF on transthoracic echocardiography were collected at 1 year, and the latest follow-up was in January 2021. Cause of death was classified as cardiovascular if patients died from cardiogenic shock, heart failure, car­ diac arrest, tamponade, ventricular arrhythmia, ischaemic stroke, sudden death, or unknown cause.

Exposure The primary outcome was survival free of HTx or long-term LVAD within 1 year after ICU admission. An EMB was defined as early when performed within 48 h of ICU admission, whereas a delayed EMB was defined as having been performed after 2 days in the ICU.

Statistical analyses We followed the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) recommendations for reporting cohort studies.23

Continuous variables were expressed as median and interquartile range (IQR), and categorical variables were expressed in frequency (percentages). Categorical variables were analysed by chi-squared or Fisher exact tests, while continuous variables were assessed by t-test or Mann–Whitney for normal and non-normal distribution, respectively, in the case of two groups analyses. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) or Kruskal–Wallis tests were used for three group analyses.

Associations between patients’ demographics, clinical and pre-t-MCS characteristics, laboratory results, and complications according to the tim­ ing of EMB were tested in univariate analyses. Two multivariable logistic re­ gression models were used to identify variables independently associated with HTx/LVAD-free survival at 1 year in (i) the whole population of pa­ tients with clinically suspected FM (Model 1; n = 419) and (ii) patients with EMB-proven myocarditis (Model 2; n = 183), respectively. The vari­ ables entered in the multivariable model were defined a priori based on clin­ ical relevance and previously published data,8,10,14,16,24–28 regardless of their P-value in univariate analysis (see Supplementary data online, Methods S1).

Variable selection was done through a backward stepwise conditional method. The results were expressed as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and P-values from a Wald test. The goodness of fit of the model was validated by omnibus tests of model coefficients at the 5% level of significance and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Multi-collinearity was assessed by calculating a variance inflation factor of each variable and ruled out if the variance inflation factor was lower than 2.

One-year survival free from HTx/LVAD was estimated by the Kaplan– Meier (KM) method for patients receiving early EMB and delayed EMB and compared with a log-rank test. A propensity score-weighted analysis was done for EMB-effect estimation. This method, which weights each pa­ tient according to their propensity score, includes the early EMB group (n = 103) and the delayed EMB group (n = 80). Based on the results of the logis­ tic regression to predict the conditional probability of 1-year mortality or HTx/LVAD and pre-specified covariates, the balance between the two groups was assessed after weighting, and an absolute standardized differ­ ence of less than 0.2 was considered as evidence of balance. The covariates used in the propensity analysis are reported in Supplementary data online,

Methods S1. Weighted-effect coding was applied for the categorical vari­ ables. The propensity scores were estimated by a logistic regression model. Adjusted KM estimator and log-rank test (considering the weighting scheme) were used. Multiple imputations were used to replace missing va­ lues when appropriate. Ten copies of the data set were created with the missing values replaced by imputed values, based on observed data of base­ line characteristics of participants. Each data set was then analysed, and the results were pooled into a final result using Rubin’s rule.29

A two-sided P-value of ≤.05 was considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were done using SPSS (version 28.0).

The median time between cardiac symptom onset and ICU admission was 3 (0–7) days. The first echocardiography showed a median LVEF of 20%, with right ventricular systolic dysfunction and pericardial effusion identified in 50% and 44% of patients, respectively.

Histologic evidence of myocarditis was confirmed in 210 (50%) pa­ tients, either on EMB (n = 183, 44%) or on explanted heart/postmortem examination (n = 27, 6%). Among patients with EMB-proven myocarditis (n = 183), the main histologies were as follows: lymphocyt­ ic myocarditis (n = 125, 68%), GCM (n = 20, 11%), eosinophilic myo­ carditis (n = 20, 11%), and other histologic subtypes (n = 18, 10%). Microbiological research using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on EMB samples was done in 75 (41%) patients. Among them, 61 (81%) had a negative result, and 14 (19%) had a positive one. Parvovirus B19 was the most frequently isolated virus (8/14).

Among the overall population, 103 (25%) patients underwent an early EMB, whereas 80 (19%) and 236 (56%) had delayed and no EMB, respectively. When comparing these three groups, baseline char­ acteristics, clinical presentation, and severity of FM were largely similar (Table 1). Histologic subtypes of myocarditis did not differ between early and delayed EMB groups.

In-hospital events Among the 419 patients with clinically suspected FM, 97 (23%) required inotropic agents only, 27 (6%) IABP alone, and 295 (70%) VA-ECMO and/or Impella®, respectively (Table 2). VA-ECMO was the most com­ mon t-MCS strategy (70%), initiated 0 (0–1) days after ICU admission.

While there was no difference in the composite use of t-MCS in early EMB, delayed EMB, and no EMB groups (77%, 82%, and 75% re­ spectively, P = .389), the early EMB group less frequently received VA-ECMO/Impella® (P = .013) (Table 2).

Only six episodes of tamponade were deemed related to EMB, re­ presenting only 3% of the EMB procedures (Table 2). Death was not attributed to any of these six events.

One-year outcomes and associated risk factors The overall survival free of HTx or LVAD was 65% at 1 year. Among patients who died (n = 116, 28%) or underwent HTx (n = 30, 7%) or LVAD implantation (n = 20, 5%) in the first year, the median time to event was 44 days (19–82) (Table 2).

Among patients with EMB-proven myocarditis (n = 183), early EMB was associated with an unadjusted higher rate of survival free of HTx/ LVAD at 1 year compared with delayed EMB (70% vs. 49%, P = .004; Figure 2). After propensity score weighting, early EMB was still asso­ ciated with a significantly better survival free from HTx/LVAD (63% vs. 40%, P = .021) (Table 3 and Figure 2). Furthermore, in the subgroup of patients with lymphocytic myocarditis (n = 125, 68%), early EMB was associated with a better prognosis compared with delayed EMB as well (72% vs. 50% P = .013; Figure 3A). A similar trend was observed for eo­ sinophilic myocarditis (91% vs. 56%, P = .052; Figure 3B). Giant cell myo­ carditis had significantly worse outcomes than other aetiologies, with 1-year survival free of HTx/LVAD of only 25% (P = .006), regardless of the EMB timing (Figure 3C and D).

Predictors of 1-year survival free of HTx/LVAD were assessed in the whole population with clinically suspected FM (n = 419) (see Supplementary data online, Table S2) and in patients with EMB-proven myocarditis (n = 183) (Table 4). Among this latter popula­ tion, sinus rhythm and higher lactates at ICU admission were independ­ ently associated with the primary outcome at 1 year. Additionally, early EMB was associated with a lower likelihood of death, HTx, or LVAD [OR 0.44 (0.22–0.86); P = .016] (Table 4).

Immunomodulatory therapies Among the entire cohort, 186 (44%) patients received IMT during their ICU stay of whom 177 (95%) received corticosteroids, 49 (26%) an­ other immunomodulatory agent, and 42 (23%) intravenous immuno­ globulins (IVIG) (Table 2). ## Discussion

The FULLMOON registry is one of the largest series to date, with de­ tailed data on patients’ characteristics at ICU admission, further identi­ fying prognostic factors that can promptly stratify patients at high risk of death or need for HTx or LVAD. This contemporary international registry highlights that HTx/LVAD-free survival from FM is unaccept­ ably low, despite an enrolment of cases exclusively from high-volume ECMO centres (Structured Graphical Abstract). Despite FM being a re­ versible cause of cardiogenic shock7,30 and the relatively young median age in this cohort (40 years), 1-year survival free of HTx/LVAD was only 65%. Given that early recognition and accurate histologic identification of FM are considered cornerstones to reducing mortality, EMB is re­ commended in adult patients with FM.4–7,11,12 After using propensity score weighting, early EMB shows significantly better survival free of HTx/LVAD compared with delayed EMB. These results are in line with those from a recent multi-centre Japanese cohort that reports that no EMB is independently associated with poorer outcomes com­ pared with patients who underwent EMB.13 Furthermore, beyond as­ sessing myocarditis diagnosis, early EMB could allow for rapid identification of the most severe patients based on the extent of myo­ cardial damage on EMB samples. Another recent large cohort study found that myocardial damage accounting for >50% of EMB samples is associated with an increased risk of 90-day death or HTx in patients with lymphocytic myocarditis.31 Thus, early EMB appears to be the best way to rapidly confirm the diagnosis, identify the histologic subtype, as­ sess the severity of FM, and initiate specific treatment.6,7,32

Inappropriate treatment with IMT without systematic diagnosis con­ firmation by EMB may expose this critically ill population to severe in­ fectious complications. Among patients with lymphocytic myocarditis, those with early EMB and receiving early IMT had a better survival free of HTx/LVAD at 1 year. Likewise, a significant trend was also ob­ served in eosinophilic myocarditis, even if it did not reach statistical sig­ nificance, likely due to the small sample size of this histologic subtype (only 20 cases). Except in eosinophilic myocarditis,33,34 GCM,35 or some subsets of lymphocytic myocarditis, including systemic auto­ immune disease32 and immune check-point inhibitors’ toxicity,36 the benefits of IMT on survival in FM remain undefined. Historical rando­ mized controlled trials failed to demonstrate a reduction in mortality with IMT37–39 in non-fulminant lymphocytic myocarditis, although it might be associated with a quicker improvement of LVEF.39 Recent in­ sights from the 20-year follow-up of patients with virus-free active myocarditis proven on EMB, originally included in the TIMIC study,39

pointed out a significantly higher HTx-free survival for those treated with corticosteroids plus azathioprine.40 However, all of these studies focused on chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathies with symptoms lasting for more than 3–6 months, making it difficult to extrapolate these results to fulminant forms. Randomized controlled trials are therefore urgently warranted to assess the efficacy of IMT, especially corticosteroids in lymphocytic FM32 (NCT05150704).

Endomyocardial biopsy is also the only way to identify GCM, which is associated with a low HTx/LVAD-free survival at 1 year, consistent with previous reports.1,10,41 Indeed, Cooper et al.42 historically re­ ported an 89% rate of death or HTx within 5 months from the onset of symptoms, whereas the rate of in-hospital death or HTx was 100% in a French registry of GCM on VA-ECMO.41 However, prompt use of a combined heavy regimen of IMT, using two to four drugs in­ cluding corticosteroids, seems to improve outcomes.35 Accordingly, more recent registries of GCM, in which at least 70% of the patients have been treated with triple immunosuppression, report better out­ comes with a rate of 5-year HTx-free survival since the onset of symp­ toms between 42% and 52%.43,44 However, fulminant forms were under-represented in these studies. Thus, early EMB may be particularly crucial to rapidly diagnose fulminant GCM and start specific treatment.

To further stress the high-risk profile of our cohort, 70% received t-MCS other than IABP, while in the previous co­ hort, it was only 51%.10 Only four recent multi-centre cohorts with more than 100 cases of FM identified factors associated with progno­ sis.8,10,13,31 We showed that increased lactate or renal function impair­ ment on Day 1 was independently associated with prognosis, whereas sinus rhythm was associated with better outcomes. These findings are consistent with the CHANGE PUMP 2 registry and the Japanese Registry of Fulminant Myocarditis where ventricular arrhythmias and a non-sinus rhythm at presentation were associated with worse out­ comes.13,31 Other factors such as a QRS duration > 120 ms, GCM on histology, and the need for t-MCS other than IABP were independ­ ently associated with poor outcomes.10

The study has several limitations. First, its retrospective nature across 36 centres over 12 years may have led to variations in patient management both by centre and over time. To limit the impact of these potential confounders, we included only international centres with me­ dium to high t-MCS case volume.49 However, restriction to such cen­ tres may overestimate the need for t-MCS in FM and limit the generalizability of our findings. Second, to fully describe real-world out­ comes of FM, we included patients with clinically suspected myocarditis (i.e. not proven by EMB or CMRI). The risk of misdiagnosis was mini­ mized by applying a consistent definition of FM with the review of all cases by three independent investigators.
